scenario_title: Build a real-time transaction fraud scoring model under strict latency and fairness constraints
context: A payments platform processes 50,000 transactions per minute and wants to replace its rules-based fraud detection system with an ML model. The rules system has a false positive rate of 1.8% — blocking legitimate transactions — and a false negative rate of 0.4% — missing actual fraud. The model must score every transaction in real time before it is approved. The platform operates in Vietnam and Thailand, where fraud patterns differ significantly by market, and the Data Science team has flagged that historical fraud labels are noisy — some 'fraud' labels were disputes later resolved as legitimate.
the_problem: Design an ML-based fraud scoring system that improves on the current rules system's false positive rate while maintaining or improving the false negative rate, operating at 50,000 transactions per minute with sub-100ms inference.
constraints: Sub-100ms inference latency — the fraud score must be returned before the transaction is approved; batch inference is not an option

Fraud labels in training data are noisy — an estimated 15% of 'fraud' labels are incorrect (disputed transactions later reversed); the model must account for label noise rather than treating all labels as ground truth
The model must not disproportionately decline transactions from users in lower-income segments — the platform has a financial inclusion mandate and regulators have flagged this risk
The rules-based system will run in parallel during a transition period; the ML model's output must be reconcilable with the rules system for audit purposes

coach_notes.strong_response_pattern: Strong candidates surface the label noise problem as the most important modelling challenge — standard cross-entropy loss will overfit to noisy labels, and they propose techniques such as label smoothing, noise-robust loss functions (e.g., symmetric cross-entropy), or confident learning to identify and down-weight likely mislabelled examples. They address latency by proposing a gradient boosted tree model (XGBoost/LightGBM) rather than a deep learning model — trees have sub-millisecond inference at this scale. They propose market-specific models or market as a feature with interaction terms to address Vietnam/Thailand pattern divergence. For the financial inclusion constraint, they propose monitoring false positive rates by income segment and potentially using a fairness-aware threshold calibration per segment. They address the parallel running period by designing the output as a probability score (not a binary decision) so it can be combined with rule outputs via a logic layer.
common_failure_patterns: Not addressing label noise at all — accepting all historical fraud labels as ground truth and designing a standard classification pipeline, which will inherit the noise into the model

Proposing a deep learning model (LSTM for sequential transaction data) without addressing the latency constraint — an LSTM serving 50,000 TPS at sub-100ms is an infrastructure problem most candidates do not resolve
coach_notes.coaching_pressure_points: Step 1 (Define) — the label noise constraint is the hardest to surface because it is embedded in a subordinate clause. Most candidates read past it. Push them: 'You mentioned you'd train on historical fraud labels. What do you know about the quality of those labels?' until they engage with the 15% noise estimate and its implications for model design.

scenario_title: Build a quiz question difficulty estimator for adaptive assessments
context: An Edtech platform runs in-course quizzes to assess learner understanding. Currently, all quiz questions are manually tagged as Easy, Medium, or Hard by content authors — a process that is slow, inconsistent, and subjective. The platform wants to use ML to automatically estimate question difficulty so that quizzes can be dynamically calibrated to each learner's level. The platform has 3 years of learner response data.
the_problem: Design a model that estimates the difficulty level of a quiz question (Easy / Medium / Hard) based on question content and historical learner response data.
constraints: The model must handle new questions with no response history — not all questions have been attempted yet; cold-start for new content must be addressed explicitly
The difficulty estimate must be explainable to content authors who review and override it — a black-box score is not sufficient for the content team's workflow
Questions span 8 subject domains (Math, Science, English, etc.); difficulty is domain-relative — a 'Hard' Math question and a 'Hard' English question are not directly comparable
supporting_data: 3 years of response data: 2 million question-attempt records with correct/incorrect outcomes
10,000 unique questions currently in the platform; 500 new questions added per month
Current author-tag agreement rate: 68% when two authors independently tag the same question

coach_notes.strong_response_pattern: Candidate proposes a hybrid approach: for questions with response history, use Item Response Theory (IRT) or a response-based difficulty score (e.g., average correctness rate, adjusted for learner ability). For cold-start questions, use NLP features from the question text (length, vocabulary complexity, number of reasoning steps) to predict difficulty. They address domain-relativity by training separate models per domain or using domain as a feature with interaction terms. For explainability, they propose surfacing the top contributing features (e.g., 'This question scored Hard because 78% of learners who attempted it answered incorrectly and the vocabulary complexity score is in the top 15% for Math questions').
common_failure_patterns: Designing only a response-based model without addressing cold-start — leaving 500 new questions per month with no difficulty estimate until enough response data accumulates
Proposing a single model across all domains without addressing domain-relativity — a model trained on all domains will conflate difficulty signals across subjects
coach_notes.coaching_pressure_points: Step 2 (Decompose) — push candidates to separate the two prediction pathways: (a) questions with response history and (b) new questions without history. Most candidates default to a single model and only address the cold-start problem when prompted.

Questions span 8 subject domains. Difficulty estimates must be explainable to content authors. How would you design this model?

scenario_title: Build a personalised content recommendation engine
context: An Edtech platform hosts 3,000 learning units across 120 courses. Learners currently browse and select content randomly, resulting in low completion rates and non-sequential learning paths. The platform wants to build a recommendation engine that surfaces the next best learning unit for each learner — based on their learning history, performance, and curriculum structure. The team believes a well-sequenced path will improve 30-day retention.
the_problem: Design a recommendation system that surfaces the next best learning unit for each learner, balancing curriculum sequencing logic with personalised learning pace and interest signals.
constraints: Cold-start problem: 40% of active users have fewer than 3 completed learning units — collaborative filtering alone will not work for these users
The platform has explicit curriculum prerequisites — Unit B cannot be recommended before Unit A is completed; the model must respect hard sequencing rules, not just optimise for engagement
Recommendations must not create filter bubbles — learners should not be trapped in a narrow content loop; the system must expose learners to new topic areas periodically
supporting_data: 3,000 learning units; average unit length: 18 minutes
User base: 80,000 active learners; median completed units per user: 7
Completion rate for recommended units vs. self-selected units in a previous A/B test: 54% vs. 41%
40% of users have fewer than 3 completed units (cold-start segment)

coach_notes.strong_response_pattern: Candidate correctly identifies that this is not a pure collaborative filtering problem — the curriculum prerequisite constraint means recommendations must first filter the eligible set before ranking. They propose a two-stage architecture: (1) candidate generation using curriculum rules to produce an eligible set, followed by (2) a ranking model (matrix factorisation, neural collaborative filtering, or content-based features) to personalise within the eligible set. For cold-start users, they propose content-based fallback using learner self-reported goals or onboarding quiz results. For filter bubble prevention, they propose an exploration budget (e.g., 20% of recommendations are diversified picks outside the learner's dominant topic cluster). They define success metrics as completion rate and 30-day retention, not click-through rate.
common_failure_patterns: Designing a pure collaborative filtering system without addressing the prerequisite constraint — recommending advanced units to beginners because 'similar users liked them'
Treating cold-start as an edge case rather than 40% of the user base — proposing a fallback without designing it properly
coach_notes.coaching_pressure_points: Step 1 (Define) — the implicit constraint is that 'next best unit' has two competing definitions: the unit the learner is most likely to engage with, and the unit that is most educationally appropriate given their current level. Push candidates: 'How do you handle a case where the most engaging recommendation violates a curriculum prerequisite?' until they separate the eligibility filter from the ranking model.

scenario_title: Design an LLM-based Socratic tutor that adapts to learner misconceptions without giving answers away
context: An Edtech platform wants to deploy an AI tutor for secondary school students (ages 13–17) studying STEM subjects. The tutor's role is Socratic — it should guide learners to the correct answer through questions and hints, not give answers directly. A pilot of a simple GPT-4 based tutor failed: students learned to extract direct answers by rephrasing their questions (prompt injection), and the tutor occasionally generated factually incorrect explanations that students accepted as correct. The platform's pedagogy team is adamant: the tutor must never directly answer a question a student is supposed to solve independently.
the_problem: Design an LLM-based Socratic tutoring system that guides learners toward answers through adaptive questioning, resists prompt injection attempts to extract direct answers, and flags factual uncertainty rather than hallucinating confident explanations.
constraints: The system must never directly answer a problem the student is tasked with solving — even if the student phrases the request in a way that bypasses the original instruction (adversarial rephrasing and prompt injection resistance is required)

The tutor must detect learner misconceptions from their responses and adapt its guiding questions accordingly — generic 'hints' that do not reflect the specific error the student made are not acceptable
The system must operate within a strict content safety policy for minors — no generation of content outside the curriculum topic, even if a student attempts to redirect the conversation
Factual uncertainty must be flagged explicitly — when the model's confidence in a factual claim is low, it must indicate this rather than generating a plausible-sounding but incorrect explanation

coach_notes.strong_response_pattern: Strong candidates identify three distinct technical problems that must be solved independently: (1) answer-leakage prevention via prompt injection, (2) misconception detection and adaptive questioning, and (3) hallucination detection and uncertainty flagging. For (1), they propose a system prompt architecture with a constitutional AI or rule-based guardrail layer that intercepts outputs before delivery and checks whether a direct answer is present — not relying on a single system prompt instruction. For (2), they propose a two-stage pipeline: classify the student's response against a misconception taxonomy for the topic, then select a guiding question template conditioned on the detected misconception class. For (3), they propose RAG grounding against a verified curriculum knowledge base, with a confidence scoring layer that flags low-retrieval-score responses. They acknowledge that these three systems create latency and propose a streaming response architecture to mask it.
common_failure_patterns: Proposing a single system prompt with instructions like 'never give direct answers' as the primary defence against prompt injection — this is precisely what failed in the pilot and demonstrates misunderstanding of LLM adversarial robustness
Treating misconception detection as a simple 'wrong answer' flag rather than a taxonomy of specific error types — this produces generic hints that do not address the student's actual reasoning error
coach_notes.coaching_pressure_points: Step 1 (Define) — the framing trap is treating this as a 'better prompt engineering' problem. The pilot already used a good system prompt and it failed. Push candidates: 'The pilot used GPT-4 with clear instructions not to give answers. Students bypassed it. What does that tell you about the limits of prompt-only solutions?' until they get to the need for a programmatic guardrail layer separate from the LLM prompt.

scenario_title: Build an automated property listing quality scorer
context: A property rental platform has a problem with low-quality listings — missing photos, incomplete descriptions, and vague location details — that reduce renter trust and increase time-to-rent for landlords. The platform wants to build an automated quality scorer that rates each listing at submission time and prompts landlords to improve weak areas before publishing. The product team has access to historical listing data and renter engagement metrics.
the_problem: Design a model that scores a newly submitted property listing's quality on a scale of 1–10 and identifies the specific weaknesses that should be flagged to the landlord.
constraints: The scorer must produce actionable feedback — a score alone is not sufficient; the system must identify which specific fields are dragging the score down so the landlord knows what to fix
The model must run at submission time with under 2 seconds response latency — landlords should not wait for a score after clicking 'Submit'
The platform has both Vietnamese and English listing descriptions; the quality model must handle both languages without a separate preprocessing pipeline for each
supporting_data: Historical data: 150,000 published listings with renter engagement metrics (views, enquiry rate, time-to-first-enquiry)
Average listing fields: 12 structured fields (price, area, bedrooms, etc.) + free-text description + up to 20 photos
Listings with 8+ photos receive 2.4× more enquiries than listings with fewer than 3 photos
Listings with descriptions over 100 words receive 1.8× more enquiries than listings under 30 words

coach_notes.strong_response_pattern: Candidate correctly frames this as a supervised regression or classification problem using renter engagement (enquiry rate, time-to-first-enquiry) as the proxy label for quality — not using a manufactured quality label. They propose a feature set covering structured completeness (% of fields filled), photo count and quality (using a pre-trained image quality model), and text quality signals (description length, language detection, readability). For actionable feedback, they propose a feature attribution layer (SHAP or simple rule-based thresholds per feature) that identifies the lowest-scoring components. They address multilingual text by proposing a multilingual embedding model (mBERT or LaBSE) rather than language-specific models.
common_failure_patterns: Proposing to use a manually created 'quality' label rather than the engagement proxy signal — asking who creates the ground truth labels without recognising that renter behaviour is the more reliable signal
Designing a model that outputs a single score without the attribution layer — missing the core product requirement that the landlord must know what to fix
coach_notes.coaching_pressure_points: Step 2 (Decompose) — push candidates on label definition: 'What is the ground truth label for a high-quality listing?' If they say 'a human-labelled quality score', push back: 'Who labels 150,000 listings and what do they use as their criteria?' Guide them toward renter engagement as the business-grounded proxy label.

scenario_title: Build a rental price recommendation engine for new listings
context: A property rental platform wants to help landlords price their listings competitively. Overpriced listings sit unrented; underpriced listings lose landlord revenue and reduce platform GMV. The platform wants to show each new landlord a recommended price range at the point of listing creation, based on comparable properties. The team has 3 years of listing and rental transaction data across Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi.
the_problem: Design a model that recommends an optimal rental price range for a new listing, given its attributes and comparable properties in the same area.
constraints: New landlords have no historical listings on the platform — cold-start must be handled explicitly; the model cannot rely on the landlord's own price history
The recommendation must be a price range, not a point estimate — landlords need to understand the uncertainty; a confident wrong point estimate erodes trust more than a wide honest range

The model must be interpretable to landlords — a landlord who receives a lower-than-expected recommendation must be able to understand why (e.g., 'Similar 2-bedroom units in Tân Bình currently rent for 8–10M VND; yours is slightly below average area')
supporting_data: 3 years of data: 85,000 listings with final agreed rental prices, listing attributes, and days-to-rent
Feature set: district, ward, area (sqm), number of bedrooms/bathrooms, floor, amenities (parking, balcony, etc.), listing photos (available but not currently used)
Seasonal price variance: HCMC rental prices fluctuate ~12% between peak (September–November) and low season (February–April)
Data sparsity: 40 of 88 districts in HCMC have fewer than 50 historical listings

coach_notes.strong_response_pattern: Candidate identifies this as a hedonic pricing model problem — predicting price from property attributes. They propose a gradient boosted tree (XGBoost/LightGBM) or a quantile regression model — quantile regression naturally outputs prediction intervals (e.g., 10th–90th percentile) rather than point estimates, directly addressing the range requirement. They address sparse districts by proposing geographic hierarchical features (ward → district → city) and potentially a spatial similarity model for data-sparse areas. They address cold-start by noting that the model is property-based, not landlord-based — cold-start here means a new property type or area, not a new landlord. For interpretability, they propose SHAP values with natural language templates ('Your property scores lower on amenities than comparable listings'). They flag seasonal adjustment as a necessary post-processing step.
common_failure_patterns: Misidentifying cold-start as a landlord history problem — the model is trained on property attributes, not landlord identity, so there is no true landlord cold-start. Candidates who spend time on landlord embeddings have misread the constraint
Proposing a point estimate model and adding ±X%
